claim: Pancreas-specific deletion of Adrb2 results in glucose intolerance in female mice.
source: Pancreas-specific deletion of Adrb2 results in glucose intolerance and impaired insulin secretion in mice, and unexpectedly, specifically in females.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data showing elevated blood glucose levels in female Adrb2 cKO mice compared to controls (Figure 1A-B).

claim: Pancreas-specific deletion of Adrb2 results in impaired insulin secretion in female mice.
source: Pancreas-specific deletion of Adrb2 results in glucose intolerance and impaired insulin secretion in mice, and unexpectedly, specifically in females.
evidence: Supported by in vivo insulin secretion measurements showing reduced insulin levels during glucose challenge in female Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 1E).

claim: The metabolic phenotypes of Adrb2 deletion are sex-specific, occurring only in females.
source: Pancreas-specific deletion of Adrb2 results in glucose intolerance and impaired insulin secretion in mice, and unexpectedly, specifically in females.
evidence: Supported by data showing normal glucose tolerance and insulin secretion in male Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 1C, D, F).

claim: The metabolic phenotypes were recapitulated by Adrb2 deletion from neonatal, but not adult, β-cells.
source: The metabolic phenotypes were recapitulated by Adrb2 deletion from neonatal, but not adult, β-cells.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance and insulin secretion data from tamoxifen-inducible Adrb2 deletion experiments at different developmental stages (Figure 1I-K and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L-O).

claim: Adrb2 loss increases production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-A (VEGF-A) in female neonatal β-cells.
source: Mechanistically, Adrb2 loss increases production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-A (VEGF-A) in female neonatal β-cells and results in hyper-vascularized islets during development, which in turn, disrupts insulin production and exocytosis.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing increased Vegfa mRNA in Adrb2 cKO pancreas and purified β-cells (Figure 2J, K).

claim: Adrb2 loss results in hyper-vascularized islets during development.
source: Mechanistically, Adrb2 loss increases production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-A (VEGF-A) in female neonatal β-cells and results in hyper-vascularized islets during development, which in turn, disrupts insulin production and exocytosis.
evidence: Supported by PECAM1 immunostaining showing increased intra-islet vasculature in neonatal Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2E, F).

claim: Islet hyper-vascularization disrupts insulin production in Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Mechanistically, Adrb2 loss increases production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-A (VEGF-A) in female neonatal β-cells and results in hyper-vascularized islets during development, which in turn, disrupts insulin production and exocytosis.
evidence: Supported by increased insulin immunoreactivity and content in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), and rescue of insulin transcript levels by VEGFR2 blockade (Figure 4C).

claim: Islet hyper-vascularization disrupts insulin exocytosis in Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Mechanistically, Adrb2 loss increases production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-A (VEGF-A) in female neonatal β-cells and results in hyper-vascularized islets during development, which in turn, disrupts insulin production and exocytosis.
evidence: Supported by impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Figure 1G), reduced insulin granule docking (Figure 3B, C), and decreased expression of exocytosis machinery genes (Figure 3F).

claim: Neonatal correction of islet hyper-vascularization via VEGF-A receptor blockade fully rescues functional deficits in glucose homeostasis in adult mutant mice.
source: Neonatal correction of islet hyper-vascularization, via VEGF-A receptor blockade, fully rescues functional deficits in glucose homeostasis in adult mutant mice.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance and insulin secretion data from VEGFR2 antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Global Adrb2 knockout mice exhibit impaired glucose tolerance at 6 months.
source: Global Adrb2 knockout mice exhibit impaired glucose tolerance and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) at 6 months (Santulli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Global Adrb2 knockout mice exhibit impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) at 6 months.
source: Global Adrb2 knockout mice exhibit impaired glucose tolerance and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) at 6 months (Santulli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: β-adrenergic agonists augment circulating insulin levels in humans.
source: In humans, β-adrenergic agonists augment circulating insulin levels, and stimulate insulin secretion from isolated islets (Ahrén and Scherstén, 1986; Lacey et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: β-adrenergic agonists stimulate insulin secretion from isolated human islets.
source: In humans, β-adrenergic agonists augment circulating insulin levels, and stimulate insulin secretion from isolated islets (Ahrén and Scherstén, 1986; Lacey et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Pdx1-Cre;Adrb2f/f mice were born at expected Mendelian frequencies.
source: Pdx1-Cre;Adrb2f/f mice (henceforth referred to as Adrb2 cKO mice) were born at expected Mendelian frequencies, had normal body weight at birth, no gross morphological abnormalities, and survived to adulthood.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Adrb2 cKO mice had normal body weight at birth.
source: Pdx1-Cre;Adrb2f/f mice (henceforth referred to as Adrb2 cKO mice) were born at expected Mendelian frequencies, had normal body weight at birth, no gross morphological abnormalities, and survived to adulthood.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Adrb2 cKO mice had no gross morphological abnormalities.
source: Pdx1-Cre;Adrb2f/f mice (henceforth referred to as Adrb2 cKO mice) were born at expected Mendelian frequencies, had normal body weight at birth, no gross morphological abnormalities, and survived to adulthood.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Adrb2 cKO mice survived to adulthood.
source: Pdx1-Cre;Adrb2f/f mice (henceforth referred to as Adrb2 cKO mice) were born at expected Mendelian frequencies, had normal body weight at birth, no gross morphological abnormalities, and survived to adulthood.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Significant Adrb2 reduction was observed in Adrb2 cKO pancreas at postnatal day 6 (P6).
source: Significant Adrb2 reduction was observed in Adrb2 cKO pancreas assessed at postnatal day 6 (P6) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Female Adrb2 cKO mice are glucose intolerant at 2 months of age.
source: Surprisingly, we found that only female Adrb2 cKO mice were glucose intolerant, while male Adrb2 cKO mice exhibited normal glucose tolerance (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Male Adrb2 cKO mice exhibited normal glucose tolerance at 2 months of age.
source: Surprisingly, we found that only female Adrb2 cKO mice were glucose intolerant, while male Adrb2 cKO mice exhibited normal glucose tolerance (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance test data in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Female Adrb2 cKO mice showed reduced insulin secretion during the first phase of the glucose challenge (measured 5 min after the glucose challenge).
source: Female Adrb2 cKO mice also showed reduced insulin secretion during the first phase of the glucose challenge (measured 5 min after the glucose challenge), as well as dampened insulin levels in the sustained second phase (30 min after the glucose challenge) compared to same-sex control mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo insulin secretion data in Figure 1E.

claim: Female Adrb2 cKO mice showed dampened insulin levels in the sustained second phase (30 min after the glucose challenge).
source: Female Adrb2 cKO mice also showed reduced insulin secretion during the first phase of the glucose challenge (measured 5 min after the glucose challenge), as well as dampened insulin levels in the sustained second phase (30 min after the glucose challenge) compared to same-sex control mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo insulin secretion data in Figure 1E.

claim: Glucose-induced insulin secretion was unaffected in male Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: In contrast, glucose-induced insulin secretion was unaffected in male Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by in vivo insulin secretion data in Figure 1F.

claim: Control males showed lower glucose tolerance relative to control females.
source: Consistent with previous studies in mice (Gannon et al., 2018; Goren et al., 2004; Lavine et al., 1971), control males showed lower glucose tolerance relative to control females (compare Figure 1A,B versus 1C,D), and also lower glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (compare Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by comparison of glucose tolerance data between male and female control mice in Figure 1, and consistent with cited literature.

claim: Control males showed lower glucose-stimulated insulin secretion relative to control females.
source: Consistent with previous studies in mice (Gannon et al., 2018; Goren et al., 2004; Lavine et al., 1971), control males showed lower glucose tolerance relative to control females (compare Figure 1A,B versus 1C,D), and also lower glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (compare Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by comparison of insulin secretion data between male and female control mice in Figure 1E and F, and consistent with cited literature.

claim: Similar depletion (~90% decrease) of Adrb2 mRNA was found in male and female mutant islets relative to same-sex controls.
source: Using qPCR analyses, we found similar depletion (~90% decrease) of Adrb2 mRNA from male and female mutant islets relative to same-sex controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating that absence of metabolic phenotypes in male mutant mice is not due to inefficient Adrb2 deletion.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Absence of metabolic phenotypes in male mutant mice is not due to inefficient Adrb2 deletion.
source: Using qPCR analyses, we found similar depletion (~90% decrease) of Adrb2 mRNA from male and female mutant islets relative to same-sex controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), indicating that absence of metabolic phenotypes in male mutant mice is not due to inefficient Adrb2 deletion.
evidence: Inference based on qPCR data showing similar Adrb2 depletion in both sexes.

claim: Both male and female Adrb2 cKO mice showed normal insulin sensitivity.
source: Both male and female Adrb2 cKO mice showed normal insulin sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that the glucose intolerance in female Adrb2 cKO mice does not stem from defects in insulin responsiveness.
evidence: Supported by insulin sensitivity test data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The glucose intolerance in female Adrb2 cKO mice does not stem from defects in insulin responsiveness.
source: Both male and female Adrb2 cKO mice showed normal insulin sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting that the glucose intolerance in female Adrb2 cKO mice does not stem from defects in insulin responsiveness.
evidence: Inference based on normal insulin sensitivity data.

claim: Both basal and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion were significantly blunted in adult female Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Both basal and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion were significantly blunted in adult female Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by in vitro insulin secretion data from isolated islets in Figure 1G.

claim: Islet shape and cyto-architecture were unaffected by pancreatic Adrb2 loss.
source: These analyses revealed the stereotypical arrangement of insulin-producing β-cells at the core surrounded by glucagon-producing α-cells at the periphery or mantle in both control and Adrb2 mutant islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that islet shape and cyto-architecture were unaffected by pancreatic Adrb2 loss.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Insulin immunoreactivity was increased in adult Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Intriguingly, we observed an increase in insulin immunoreactivity in adult Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Enhanced insulin expression in mutant islets was confirmed by ELISA.
source: Enhanced insulin expression in mutant islets was confirmed by ELISA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Islet insulin content is increased with pancreatic Adrb2 deletion, despite a profound reduction in insulin secretion.
source: These results indicate that islet insulin content is increased with pancreatic Adrb2 deletion, despite a profound reduction in insulin secretion (see Figure 1G).
evidence: Inference based on ELISA and insulin secretion data.

claim: Adult Adrb2 mutant islets had normal endocrine cell numbers.
source: Morphometric analyses revealed normal endocrine cell numbers in adult Adrb2 mutant islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), although the mutants had a greater distribution of smaller islets relative to control Adrb2f/f mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by morphometric analysis data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Adrb2 mutants had a greater distribution of smaller islets relative to control Adrb2f/f mice.
source: Morphometric analyses revealed normal endocrine cell numbers in adult Adrb2 mutant islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), although the mutants had a greater distribution of smaller islets relative to control Adrb2f/f mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by islet size distribution data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: There were no significant differences in the number of EdU/insulin double-positive cells between Adrb2 cKO and control adult islets.
source: Despite smaller islets, there were no significant differences in the number of EdU/insulin double-positive cells between Adrb2 cKO and control islets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, J.

claim: The percentage of replicating β-cells in both Adrb2 cKO and control adult islets was low (<1%).
source: The percentage of replicating β-cells in both Adrb2 cKO and control adult islets was low (<1%), consistent with previous studies (Puri et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling data and consistent with cited literature.

claim: The metabolic phenotypes with pancreatic Adrb2 deletion do not arise from alterations in islet architecture, β-cell mass, or diminished insulin production.
source: Together, these results suggest that the metabolic phenotypes with pancreatic Adrb2 deletion do not arise from alterations in islet architecture, β-cell mass, or diminished insulin production.
evidence: Inference based on morphometric and insulin content data.

claim: Adrb2 has been reported to be enriched in β-cells at embryonic and neonatal stages.
source: Previously, Adrb2 has been reported to be enriched in β-cells at embryonic and neonatal stages, and its expression declines with age (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Adrb2 expression declines with age.
source: Previously, Adrb2 has been reported to be enriched in β-cells at embryonic and neonatal stages, and its expression declines with age (Berger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Adrb2 expression was significantly depleted in adult islets compared to neonates.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Berger et al., 2015), Adrb2 expression was significantly depleted in adult islets compared to neonates (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1H and consistent with cited literature.

claim: The postnatal decline in Adrb2 mRNA was observed in both female and male islets.
source: The postnatal decline in Adrb2 mRNA was observed in both female and male islets.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1H.

claim: Adrb2 mRNA is 4-fold higher in purified β-cells relative to the non-β-cell population at postnatal day 6 (P6).
source: We also observed that Adrb2 mRNA is 4-fold higher in purified β-cells relative to the non-β-cell population at postnatal day 6 (P6) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from FACS-purified cells in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Adrb2 acts in β-cells during a critical neonatal window to influence islet function.
source: These findings raised the possibility that Adrb2 acts in β-cells during a critical neonatal window to influence islet function.
evidence: Inference based on developmental expression pattern and timing of deletion experiments.

claim: Pdx1 expression becomes restricted to β-cells and somatostatin-expressing δ-cells after birth.
source: Pdx1 expression becomes restricted to β-cells and somatostatin-expressing δ-cells after birth (DiGruccio et al., 2016; Guz et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Tamoxifen injection in neonatal mice resulted in significant Adrb2 mRNA depletion in adult islets (86% decrease).
source: Tamoxifen injection in neonatal mice resulted in significant Adrb2 mRNA depletion in adult islets (86% decrease, p=0.01, one sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis.

claim: Neonatal loss of Adrb2 from β-cells elicited pronounced defects in glucose tolerance.
source: Neonatal loss of Adrb2 from β-cells elicited pronounced defects in glucose tolerance and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Figure 1I–K), similar to the phenotypes observed in Adrb2 cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance data in Figure 1I-K.

claim: Neonatal loss of Adrb2 from β-cells elicited pronounced defects in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
source: Neonatal loss of Adrb2 from β-cells elicited pronounced defects in glucose tolerance and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (Figure 1I–K), similar to the phenotypes observed in Adrb2 cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion data in Figure 1K.

claim: There were no significant differences in glucose tolerance between tamoxifen- and vehicle-injected adult Adrb2 i-cKO mice at 6 weeks of age.
source: Consistent with the low Adrb2 expression in adult mice, there were no significant differences in glucose tolerance or glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) between the tamoxifen- and vehicle-injected adult Adrb2 i-cKO mice at 6 weeks of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–O).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L-M.

claim: There were no significant differences in glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) between tamoxifen- and vehicle-injected adult Adrb2 i-cKO mice at 6 weeks of age.
source: Consistent with the low Adrb2 expression in adult mice, there were no significant differences in glucose tolerance or glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GSIS) between the tamoxifen- and vehicle-injected adult Adrb2 i-cKO mice at 6 weeks of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–O).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1N-O.

claim: Adrb2 is primarily required in neonatal β-cells for insulin secretion and glucose homeostasis.
source: Together, these findings indicate that Adrb2 is primarily required in neonatal β-cells for insulin secretion and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of neonatal versus adult deletion experiments.

claim: Islet formation was unaffected in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice at P6.
source: Similar to adult mutant mice, islet formation and endocrine cell numbers were unaffected in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice at P6, (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), while mutants had a greater distribution of smaller islets relative to control Adrb2f/f mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and morphometric data in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Endocrine cell numbers were unaffected in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice at P6.
source: Similar to adult mutant mice, islet formation and endocrine cell numbers were unaffected in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice at P6, (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), while mutants had a greater distribution of smaller islets relative to control Adrb2f/f mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by morphometric data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neonatal mutants had a greater distribution of smaller islets relative to control Adrb2f/f mice.
source: Similar to adult mutant mice, islet formation and endocrine cell numbers were unaffected in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice at P6, (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), while mutants had a greater distribution of smaller islets relative to control Adrb2f/f mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by islet size distribution data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: β-cell proliferation in neonatal islets was unchanged by Adrb2 deletion.
source: β-cell proliferation in neonatal islets was also unchanged by Adrb2 deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), although we noted higher β-cell proliferation in P6 islets compared to adults as expected (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Insulin immunoreactivity was increased in neonatal (P6) Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Notably, insulin immunoreactivity (Figure 2A) and islet insulin content (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) were increased in neonatal (P6) Adrb2 cKO islets, similar to the findings in adult mutant islets.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining in Figure 2A.

claim: Islet insulin content was increased in neonatal (P6) Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Notably, insulin immunoreactivity (Figure 2A) and islet insulin content (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) were increased in neonatal (P6) Adrb2 cKO islets, similar to the findings in adult mutant islets.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Insulin transcript (Ins2) levels were increased in neonatal Adrb2 cKO islets beginning two days after birth.
source: qPCR analyses revealed an increase in insulin transcript (Ins2) levels in neonatal Adrb2 cKO islets beginning two days after birth (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Ultra-structural analyses revealed a pronounced increase in insulin granule density in β-cells from Adrb2 cKO islets at P6.
source: Further, ultra-structural analyses revealed a pronounced increase in insulin granule density in β-cells from Adrb2 cKO islets at P6 (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 2C, D.

claim: Adrb2 negatively regulates insulin expression during islet development.
source: These results suggest that Adrb2 negatively regulates insulin expression during islet development.
evidence: Inference based on increased insulin transcript and protein levels in Adrb2 cKO islets.

claim: Adrb2 activation did not elicit changes in Ins2 transcript levels in MIN6 cells.
source: To ask if Adrb2 directly suppresses insulin, we stimulated cultured MIN6 cells, an insulinoma-derived cell line analogous to β-cells, with epinephrine or norepinephrine, the endogenous ligands for Adrb2, or salbutamol, an Adrb2-specific agonist. Assessment of Ins2 transcript levels showed Adrb2 activation did not elicit any changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from MIN6 cell experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The repressive effect of Adrb2 on insulin expression in β-cells is indirect.
source: These results hint that the repressive effect of Adrb2 on insulin expression in β-cells is indirect.
evidence: Inference based on lack of direct effect of Adrb2 agonists on insulin expression in MIN6 cells.

claim: Pancreatic islets are highly vascularized where endocrine cells are embedded in a dense meshwork of capillaries.
source: Pancreatic islets are highly vascularized where endocrine cells are embedded in a dense meshwork of capillaries that allows for accurate glucose sensing, provides continuous oxygen supply to facilitate high aerobic metabolism, and ensures rapid insulin secretion into the blood stream (Bonner-Weir and Orci, 1982; Eberhard et al., 2010; Hogan and Hull, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work and established knowledge.

source: The intra-islet vascular network is established during embryonic development, but undergoes pronounced expansion after birth, concomitant with endocrine cell clustering and maturation (Brissova et al., 2006; Johansson et al., 2006a).

source: Strikingly, these analyses revealed a prominent increase in intra-islet vasculature in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2E,F), similar to observations of increased insulin.
evidence: Supported by PECAM1 immunostaining data in Figure 2E, F.

claim: Intra-islet capillaries are highly fenestrated to allow for the rapid exchange of nutrients and hormones between islet-cells and the bloodstream.
source: Intra-islet capillaries are highly fenestrated to allow for the rapid exchange of nutrients and hormones between islet-cells and the bloodstream (Bearer and Orci, 1985; Henderson and Moss, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: Altered endothelial cell morphologies with thicker cell bodies were observed in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy, we observed altered endothelial cell morphologies with thicker cell bodies, fewer fenestrae, and more caveloae, which are plasma membrane invaginations involved in macromolecule transport across endothelial cells (Parton and Simons, 2007), in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Fewer fenestrae were observed in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy, we observed altered endothelial cell morphologies with thicker cell bodies, fewer fenestrae, and more caveloae, which are plasma membrane invaginations involved in macromolecule transport across endothelial cells (Parton and Simons, 2007), in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 2G-I.

source: Using transmission electron microscopy, we observed altered endothelial cell morphologies with thicker cell bodies, fewer fenestrae, and more caveloae, which are plasma membrane invaginations involved in macromolecule transport across endothelial cells (Parton and Simons, 2007), in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Caveolae are plasma membrane invaginations involved in macromolecule transport across endothelial cells.

evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

source: Islet endothelial cells also produce the vascular basement membrane, a specialized extracellular matrix consisting of collagen and laminin proteins that offer structural support, influence β-cell proliferation, and insulin gene transcription (Kaido et al., 2004; Nikolova et al., 2006; Nikolova et al., 2007).

evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: An increase in the thickness of the basement membrane was observed in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Ultra-structurally, we observed an increase in the thickness of the basement membrane in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2G), as well as enhanced immunoreactivity for Collagen IV and Laminin-411/511 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), two of the most abundant basement membrane molecules (Kaido et al., 2004; Nikolova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 2G.

claim: Enhanced immunoreactivity for Collagen IV was observed in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Ultra-structurally, we observed an increase in the thickness of the basement membrane in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2G), as well as enhanced immunoreactivity for Collagen IV and Laminin-411/511 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), two of the most abundant basement membrane molecules (Kaido et al., 2004; Nikolova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Enhanced immunoreactivity for Laminin-411/511 was observed in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Ultra-structurally, we observed an increase in the thickness of the basement membrane in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2G), as well as enhanced immunoreactivity for Collagen IV and Laminin-411/511 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), two of the most abundant basement membrane molecules (Kaido et al., 2004; Nikolova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Collagen IV and Laminin-411/511 are two of the most abundant basement membrane molecules.
source: Ultra-structurally, we observed an increase in the thickness of the basement membrane in Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 2G), as well as enhanced immunoreactivity for Collagen IV and Laminin-411/511 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), two of the most abundant basement membrane molecules (Kaido et al., 2004; Nikolova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Intra-islet capillaries have been proposed to form a scaffold to promote postnatal growth of autonomic fibers.
source: Since intra-islet capillaries have been proposed to form a scaffold to promote postnatal growth of autonomic fibers (Reinert et al., 2014), we performed Tyrosine Hydroxylase (TH) immunostaining to visualize sympathetic axons innervating Adrb2 cKO and control islets.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Sympathetic innervation in and around Adrb2 cKO islets was indistinguishable from that in control tissues.
source: Despite the pronounced increase in intra-islet endothelial cells, sympathetic innervation in and around Adrb2 cKO islets was indistinguishable from that in control tissues (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: Supported by TH immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: Adrb2 suppresses vascular growth during islet development.
source: These results suggest that Adrb2 suppresses vascular growth during islet development.
evidence: Inference based on increased vasculature in Adrb2 cKO islets.

claim: Islet hyper-vascularization does not arise from Adrb2 deletion in vascular cells.
source: Since in Adrb2 cKO mice, Pdx1-Cre activity is restricted to cells in the pancreatic anlage (Hingorani et al., 2003), we reason that islet hyper-vascularization does not arise from Adrb2 deletion in vascular cells.
evidence: Inference based on the specificity of Pdx1-Cre expression and cited literature.

claim: VEGF-A is the primary vascular mitogen in islets.
source: To understand the basis for hyper-vascularized islets in female Adrb2 cKO mice, we assessed expression of VEGF-A, the primary vascular mitogen in islets that is predominantly produced by β-cells (Brissova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: VEGF-A is predominantly produced by β-cells in islets.
source: To understand the basis for hyper-vascularized islets in female Adrb2 cKO mice, we assessed expression of VEGF-A, the primary vascular mitogen in islets that is predominantly produced by β-cells (Brissova et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: A pronounced increase (3.5 – 4.7-fold) in Vegfa mRNA was observed in Adrb2 cKO pancreas starting at two days after birth.
source: We observed a pronounced increase (3.5 – 4.7-fold) in Vegfa mRNA in Adrb2 cKO pancreas starting at two days after birth, similar to the increase in insulin expression (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2J.

claim: Mutant β-cells showed an 8-fold increase in Vegfa transcript levels compared to control β-cells.
source: Mutant β-cells showed an 8-fold increase in Vegfa transcript levels compared to control β-cells (Figure 2K).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from FACS-purified β-cells in Figure 2K.

claim: There were no differences in Vegfa mRNA between control and mutant non-β-cells.
source: There were no differences in Vegfa mRNA between control and mutant non-β-cells (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from FACS-purified non-β-cells in Figure 2L.

claim: Salbutamol significantly suppressed Vegfa mRNA levels in MIN6 cells.
source: Salbutamol and epinephrine significantly suppressed Vegfa mRNA levels, while norepinephrine had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from MIN6 cell experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Epinephrine significantly suppressed Vegfa mRNA levels in MIN6 cells.
source: Salbutamol and epinephrine significantly suppressed Vegfa mRNA levels, while norepinephrine had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from MIN6 cell experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Norepinephrine had no effect on Vegfa mRNA levels in MIN6 cells.
source: Salbutamol and epinephrine significantly suppressed Vegfa mRNA levels, while norepinephrine had no effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from MIN6 cell experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Adrb2 activity in pancreatic β-cells limits VEGF-A production during development.
source: Together, these findings provide evidence for a developmental role for pancreatic Adrb2 activity in restricting intra-islet vascular growth by limiting VEGF-A production in β-cells.
evidence: Inference based on Vegfa expression data and effects of Adrb2 agonists.

claim: Adrb2 activity restricts intra-islet vascular growth during development.
source: Together, these findings provide evidence for a developmental role for pancreatic Adrb2 activity in restricting intra-islet vascular growth by limiting VEGF-A production in β-cells.
evidence: Inference based on increased Vegfa expression and islet hyper-vascularization in Adrb2 cKO mice.

claim: Vegfa mRNA was 2.6-fold higher in neonatal (P6) male pancreata compared to females.
source: Indeed, Vegfa mRNA was 2.6-fold higher in neonatal (P6) male pancreata compared to females (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: PECAM1 immunoreactivity was increased in neonatal male islets compared to females.
source: PECAM1 immunoreactivity was also increased in neonatal male islets compared to females (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L,M).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L, M.

claim: Vegfa expression and intra-islet vasculature are higher in neonatal male islets, which inversely correlate with the lower Adrb2 expression compared to females.
source: These results suggest that Vegfa expression and intra-islet vasculature are higher in neonatal male islets, which inversely correlate with the lower Adrb2 expression compared to females.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of Vegfa, vasculature, and Adrb2 expression between sexes.

claim: Adrb2 loss had no effect on Vegfa expression in neonatal male islets.
source: Adrb2 loss had no effect on Vegfa expression or islet vasculature in neonatal male islets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–M), suggesting that male islets are less susceptible to Adrb2 loss compared to females, similar to observations of intact glucose tolerance and insulin secretion in adult male Adrb2 cKO mice (see Figure 1C,D and F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Adrb2 loss had no effect on islet vasculature in neonatal male islets.
source: Adrb2 loss had no effect on Vegfa expression or islet vasculature in neonatal male islets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–M), suggesting that male islets are less susceptible to Adrb2 loss compared to females, similar to observations of intact glucose tolerance and insulin secretion in adult male Adrb2 cKO mice (see Figure 1C,D and F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L, M.

claim: Male islets are less susceptible to Adrb2 loss compared to females.
source: Adrb2 loss had no effect on Vegfa expression or islet vasculature in neonatal male islets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K–M), suggesting that male islets are less susceptible to Adrb2 loss compared to females, similar to observations of intact glucose tolerance and insulin secretion in adult male Adrb2 cKO mice (see Figure 1C,D and F).
evidence: Inference based on lack of phenotypes in male Adrb2 cKO mice.

claim: Adult female Adrb2 cKO islets have a pronounced impairment in insulin secretion.
source: Our findings so far indicate that adult female Adrb2 cKO islets have a pronounced impairment in insulin secretion, despite elevated insulin content that is manifested as early as neonatal stages.
evidence: Summary of previous findings in the manuscript.

claim: Adult female Adrb2 cKO islets have elevated insulin content that is manifested as early as neonatal stages.
source: Our findings so far indicate that adult female Adrb2 cKO islets have a pronounced impairment in insulin secretion, despite elevated insulin content that is manifested as early as neonatal stages.
evidence: Summary of previous findings in the manuscript.

claim: Regulatory control of insulin secretion occurs at the level of glucose uptake and metabolism.
source: In β-cells, regulatory control of insulin secretion occurs at the level of glucose uptake and metabolism, β-cell plasma membrane depolarization, and insulin granule mobilization and exocytosis (MacDonald et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: Regulatory control of insulin secretion occurs at the level of β-cell plasma membrane depolarization.
source: In β-cells, regulatory control of insulin secretion occurs at the level of glucose uptake and metabolism, β-cell plasma membrane depolarization, and insulin granule mobilization and exocytosis (MacDonald et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: Regulatory control of insulin secretion occurs at the level of insulin granule mobilization and exocytosis.
source: In β-cells, regulatory control of insulin secretion occurs at the level of glucose uptake and metabolism, β-cell plasma membrane depolarization, and insulin granule mobilization and exocytosis (MacDonald et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: High potassium chloride (KCl) depolarizes the β-cell plasma membrane.
source: To address mechanisms by which Adrb2 influences islet insulin secretion, we exposed islets to high potassium chloride (KCl) which depolarizes the β-cell plasma membrane and results in the opening of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels to promote the exocytosis of secretion-ready insulin granules (Hatlapatka et al., 2009), thus by-passing the need for glucose uptake and metabolism to trigger insulin release.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: High KCl results in the opening of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels to promote the exocytosis of secretion-ready insulin granules.
source: To address mechanisms by which Adrb2 influences islet insulin secretion, we exposed islets to high potassium chloride (KCl) which depolarizes the β-cell plasma membrane and results in the opening of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels to promote the exocytosis of secretion-ready insulin granules (Hatlapatka et al., 2009), thus by-passing the need for glucose uptake and metabolism to trigger insulin release.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: High KCl by-passes the need for glucose uptake and metabolism to trigger insulin release.
source: To address mechanisms by which Adrb2 influences islet insulin secretion, we exposed islets to high potassium chloride (KCl) which depolarizes the β-cell plasma membrane and results in the opening of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels to promote the exocytosis of secretion-ready insulin granules (Hatlapatka et al., 2009), thus by-passing the need for glucose uptake and metabolism to trigger insulin release.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: A striking decrease in KCl-induced insulin secretion was observed in isolated Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: We observed a striking decrease in KCl-induced insulin secretion in isolated Adrb2 cKO islets, similar to the defects in GSIS in mutant islets (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro insulin secretion data in Figure 3A.

claim: Adrb2 regulates step(s) in insulin secretion that are at least distal to β-cell plasma membrane depolarization.
source: These findings suggest that Adrb2 regulates step(s) in insulin secretion that are at least distal to β-cell plasma membrane depolarization.
evidence: Inference based on impaired KCl-induced insulin secretion.

claim: Glucose-induced surface localization of insulin granules is impaired in Adrb2 cKO β-cells.
source: In control Adrb2f/f mice, we observed a marked increase in insulin granule localization at the β-cell plasma membrane in response to an in vivo glucose challenge compared to the fasted state (Figure 3B,C). However, glucose-induced recruitment of insulin granules to the cell surface was completely suppressed in Adrb2 cKO β-cells (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 3B, C.

claim: Adrb2 is necessary for glucose-dependent insulin granule positioning at the β-cell surface.
source: These results suggest that Adrb2 is necessary for glucose-dependent insulin granule positioning at the β-cell surface.
evidence: Inference based on impaired insulin granule docking in Adrb2 cKO β-cells.

claim: Elevation in intracellular Ca2+ concentration is a critical determinant of insulin granule exocytosis and GSIS in β-cells.
source: Elevation in intracellular Ca2+ concentration is a critical determinant of insulin granule exocytosis and GSIS in β-cells (Rorsman and Ashcroft, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: Glucose-induced enhancement of β-cell electrical activity triggers an increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels, largely via influx of extracellular Ca2+ through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Glucose-induced enhancement of β-cell electrical activity triggers an increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+ levels, largely via influx of extracellular Ca2+ through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Rorsman and Ashcroft, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: Control islets showed a robust increase in intracellular calcium in response to high glucose.
source: Control islets showed a robust increase in intracellular calcium in response to high glucose and to subsequent KCl-stimulated membrane depolarization, but in contrast, Adrb2 cKO islets showed significantly diminished calcium responsiveness under both conditions (Figure 3D,E, and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3D, E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Control islets showed a robust increase in intracellular calcium in response to KCl-stimulated membrane depolarization.
source: Control islets showed a robust increase in intracellular calcium in response to high glucose and to subsequent KCl-stimulated membrane depolarization, but in contrast, Adrb2 cKO islets showed significantly diminished calcium responsiveness under both conditions (Figure 3D,E, and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3D, E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Adrb2 cKO islets showed significantly diminished calcium responsiveness to high glucose.
source: Control islets showed a robust increase in intracellular calcium in response to high glucose and to subsequent KCl-stimulated membrane depolarization, but in contrast, Adrb2 cKO islets showed significantly diminished calcium responsiveness under both conditions (Figure 3D,E, and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3D, E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Adrb2 cKO islets showed significantly diminished calcium responsiveness to KCl.
source: Control islets showed a robust increase in intracellular calcium in response to high glucose and to subsequent KCl-stimulated membrane depolarization, but in contrast, Adrb2 cKO islets showed significantly diminished calcium responsiveness under both conditions (Figure 3D,E, and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 3D, E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: A significant down-regulation (72% decrease) in Cacna1c was observed in adult Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Notably, we observed a significant down-regulation (72% decrease) in Cacna1c which encodes for Cav1.2, the principal L-type voltage-gated calcium channel in β-cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3F.

claim: Cacna1c encodes for Cav1.2, the principal L-type voltage-gated calcium channel in β-cells.
source: Notably, we observed a significant down-regulation (72% decrease) in Cacna1c which encodes for Cav1.2, the principal L-type voltage-gated calcium channel in β-cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Established knowledge about gene function.

claim: β-cell-specific ablation of Cacna1c suppresses GSIS and elicits systemic glucose intolerance in mice.
source: Similar to findings for Adrb2 loss, β-cell-specific ablation of Cacna1c suppresses GSIS and elicits systemic glucose intolerance in mice (Schulla et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Down-regulated gene expression for components of the exocytosis apparatus in β-cells was observed in Adrb2 cKO islets, including Snap-25, Rph3al (Noc2), and Pclo (Piccolo).
source: We also observed down-regulated gene expression for components of the exocytosis apparatus in β-cells, Snap-25, Rph3al (Noc2), and Pclo (Piccolo) (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3F.

claim: Noc2 is an effector of the Rab3 and Rab27 GTPases.
source: Noc2, an effector of the Rab3 and Rab27 GTPases, is an essential component of insulin granule exocytosis (Matsumoto et al., 2004; Matsunaga et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Noc2 is an essential component of insulin granule exocytosis.
source: Noc2, an effector of the Rab3 and Rab27 GTPases, is an essential component of insulin granule exocytosis (Matsumoto et al., 2004; Matsunaga et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Piccolo is a scaffold protein that functions as a Ca2+ sensor.
source: Piccolo is a scaffold protein that functions as a Ca2+ sensor and links KATP channels, L-type calcium channels and insulin granules into exocytosis-competent complexes (Shibasaki et al., 2004), whereas Snap-25 is a t-SNARE protein that is critical for insulin granule fusion (Wheeler et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Piccolo links KATP channels, L-type calcium channels and insulin granules into exocytosis-competent complexes.
source: Piccolo is a scaffold protein that functions as a Ca2+ sensor and links KATP channels, L-type calcium channels and insulin granules into exocytosis-competent complexes (Shibasaki et al., 2004), whereas Snap-25 is a t-SNARE protein that is critical for insulin granule fusion (Wheeler et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Snap-25 is a t-SNARE protein that is critical for insulin granule fusion.
source: Piccolo is a scaffold protein that functions as a Ca2+ sensor and links KATP channels, L-type calcium channels and insulin granules into exocytosis-competent complexes (Shibasaki et al., 2004), whereas Snap-25 is a t-SNARE protein that is critical for insulin granule fusion (Wheeler et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Noc2, Pclo and Snap-25 are known to be regulated by the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor Neurod1 in β-cells.
source: Since in β-cells, Noc2, Pclo and Snap-25 are known to be regulated by the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor Neurod1 (Gu et al., 2010), we also assessed Neurod1 levels in Adrb2 cKO islets and observed a significant decrease (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: A significant decrease in Neurod1 levels was observed in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Since in β-cells, Noc2, Pclo and Snap-25 are known to be regulated by the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor Neurod1 (Gu et al., 2010), we also assessed Neurod1 levels in Adrb2 cKO islets and observed a significant decrease (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3F.

claim: The decreased Neurod1 expression in Adrb2 cKO islets suggests that β-cell maturation may be affected by Adrb2 deletion.
source: The decreased Neurod1 expression in Adrb2 cKO islets suggests that β-cell maturation may be affected by Adrb2 deletion (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: Inference based on decreased Neurod1 expression and its known role in β-cell maturation.

claim: Npy mRNA was significantly elevated in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Of these genes, we found that Npy mRNA was significantly elevated in Adrb2 cKO islets while Slc2a2 was decreased (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3F.

claim: Slc2a2 mRNA was decreased in Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Of these genes, we found that Npy mRNA was significantly elevated in Adrb2 cKO islets while Slc2a2 was decreased (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3F.

claim: Npy encodes for Neuropeptide Y (NPY), a hormone that is normally downregulated in islets during postnatal development.
source: Npy encodes for Neuropeptide Y (NPY), a hormone that is normally downregulated in islets during postnatal development (Myrsén-Axcrona et al., 1997), while its persistent expression in adult islets is associated with decreased β-cell responsiveness (Gu et al., 2010; Rodnoi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Persistent expression of NPY in adult islets is associated with decreased β-cell responsiveness.
source: Npy encodes for Neuropeptide Y (NPY), a hormone that is normally downregulated in islets during postnatal development (Myrsén-Axcrona et al., 1997), while its persistent expression in adult islets is associated with decreased β-cell responsiveness (Gu et al., 2010; Rodnoi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Slc2a2 encodes for the β-cell-specific glucose transporter, Glut2.
source: Slc2a2 encodes for the β-cell-specific glucose transporter, Glut2, which is essential for GSIS in mature β-cells (Thorens, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work and established knowledge.

claim: Glut2 is essential for GSIS in mature β-cells.
source: Slc2a2 encodes for the β-cell-specific glucose transporter, Glut2, which is essential for GSIS in mature β-cells (Thorens, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous published work.

claim: Immunostaining revealed a marked upregulation of NPY in adult Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Immunostaining also revealed a marked upregulation of NPY, and diminished Glut2 expression, in adult Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Immunostaining revealed diminished Glut2 expression in adult Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Immunostaining also revealed a marked upregulation of NPY, and diminished Glut2 expression, in adult Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no significant differences in genes involved in glycolysis between Adrb2 cKO and control islets.
source: There were no significant differences in genes involved in glycolysis (Aldob, Pfkl, Ldha, Tpi, or Pklr) or encoding for potassium channel subunits found in β-cells (Kcnj11 or Abcc8) between Adrb2 cKO and control islets (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3F.

claim: There were no significant differences in genes encoding for potassium channel subunits found in β-cells between Adrb2 cKO and control islets.
source: There were no significant differences in genes involved in glycolysis (Aldob, Pfkl, Ldha, Tpi, or Pklr) or encoding for potassium channel subunits found in β-cells (Kcnj11 or Abcc8) between Adrb2 cKO and control islets (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 3F.

claim: Impaired insulin secretion in Adrb2 cKO islets arises, in part, from decreased expression of key components of the calcium regulation and exocytotic machinery in β-cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that impaired insulin secretion in Adrb2 cKO islets arise, in part, from decreased expression of key components of the calcium regulation and exocytotic machinery in β-cells, as well as aberrant expression of specific genes associated with β-cell maturity.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression data.

claim: Impaired insulin secretion in Adrb2 cKO islets arises, in part, from aberrant expression of specific genes associated with β-cell maturity.
source: Together, these results suggest that impaired insulin secretion in Adrb2 cKO islets arise, in part, from decreased expression of key components of the calcium regulation and exocytotic machinery in β-cells, as well as aberrant expression of specific genes associated with β-cell maturity.
evidence: Inference based on gene expression data.

claim: Islet vasculature has been postulated to impact adult islet function.
source: Given that islet vasculature has been postulated to impact adult islet function (Brissova et al., 2014; Brissova et al., 2006; Cai et al., 2012), we next asked if early developmental phenotypes in VEGF-A expression and islet hyper-vascularization in Adrb2 cKO mice are causal for the later glucose intolerance and insulin secretion defects.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: VEGFR-2 (KDR or Flk-1) is the primary VEGF-A receptor expressed in intra-islet endothelial cells.
source: To test this prediction, we sought to attenuate VEGF-A signaling during development by injecting a neutralizing monoclonal antibody against VEGFR-2 (KDR or Flk-1), the primary VEGF-A receptor expressed in intra-islet endothelial cells (Brissova et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Developmental anomalies in Adrb2 cKO mice manifested at postnatal day 2 (P2).
source: Since developmental anomalies in Adrb2 cKO mice manifested at postnatal day 2 (P2), mice were injected with VEGFR2 blocking antibody every three days, starting at birth (postnatal day 0), and mice were either harvested for morphological analyses at P6, or following a final injection at P6, allowed to grow into adulthood and metabolic parameters were assessed at 2 months of age.
evidence: Based on previous data showing increased Vegfa and insulin expression at P2.

claim: Antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO mice survived to adulthood.
source: Antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO mice survived to adulthood, had normal body weight, and did not exhibit any gross morphological abnormalities.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO mice had normal body weight.
source: Antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO mice survived to adulthood, had normal body weight, and did not exhibit any gross morphological abnormalities.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: Antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO mice did not exhibit any gross morphological abnormalities.
source: Antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO mice survived to adulthood, had normal body weight, and did not exhibit any gross morphological abnormalities.
evidence: Direct observation reported in the manuscript.

claim: VEGFR2 blocking antibody administration corrected the excessive islet vascularization in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: VEGFR2 blocking antibody administration corrected the excessive islet vascularization in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4A,B), although it had no effect on elevated Vegfa expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), as expected.
evidence: Supported by PECAM1 immunostaining data in Figure 4A, B.

claim: VEGFR2 blocking antibody had no effect on elevated Vegfa expression in Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: VEGFR2 blocking antibody administration corrected the excessive islet vascularization in neonatal Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4A,B), although it had no effect on elevated Vegfa expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), as expected.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VEGFR2 neutralization normalized Ins2 transcript levels in neonatal pancreas.
source: VEGFR2 neutralization also normalized Ins2 transcript levels in neonatal pancreas (Figure 4C), suggesting that enhanced insulin expression is a consequence of aberrant VEGF-A signaling and perturbed islet vasculature in Adrb2 cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: Enhanced insulin expression is a consequence of aberrant VEGF-A signaling and perturbed islet vasculature in Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: VEGFR2 neutralization also normalized Ins2 transcript levels in neonatal pancreas (Figure 4C), suggesting that enhanced insulin expression is a consequence of aberrant VEGF-A signaling and perturbed islet vasculature in Adrb2 cKO mice.
evidence: Inference based on rescue of insulin expression by VEGFR2 blockade.

claim: Administration of the VEGFR2 blocking antibody during the first week of birth fully rescued the deficits in glucose tolerance in adult Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Remarkably, administration of the VEGFR2 blocking antibody during the first week of birth fully rescued the deficits in glucose tolerance and islet GSIS in adult Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by glucose tolerance data in Figure 4D, E.

claim: Administration of the VEGFR2 blocking antibody during the first week of birth fully rescued the deficits in islet GSIS in adult Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Remarkably, administration of the VEGFR2 blocking antibody during the first week of birth fully rescued the deficits in glucose tolerance and islet GSIS in adult Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by insulin secretion data in Figure 4F.

claim: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Cacna1c in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Cacna1c, Pclo, Rph3al, Snap25, Neurod1 and Npy in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Pclo in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Cacna1c, Pclo, Rph3al, Snap25, Neurod1 and Npy in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Rph3al in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Cacna1c, Pclo, Rph3al, Snap25, Neurod1 and Npy in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Snap25 in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Cacna1c, Pclo, Rph3al, Snap25, Neurod1 and Npy in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Neurod1 in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Cacna1c, Pclo, Rph3al, Snap25, Neurod1 and Npy in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Npy in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice.
source: Neutralizing VEGFR2 activity at neonatal stages restored the expression of Cacna1c, Pclo, Rph3al, Snap25, Neurod1 and Npy in islets isolated from 2 month old Adrb2 cKO mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4G.

claim: Immunostaining analyses revealed normal Glut2 expression in VEGFR2 neutralizing antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Additionally, immunostaining analyses revealed normal Glut2 and NPY expression in VEGFR2 neutralizing antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Immunostaining analyses revealed normal NPY expression in VEGFR2 neutralizing antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO islets.
source: Additionally, immunostaining analyses revealed normal Glut2 and NPY expression in VEGFR2 neutralizing antibody-injected Adrb2 cKO islets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a causal link between Adrb2-mediated control of the intra-islet vasculature via regulating VEGF-A expression during development and the later effects on adult β-cell function and glucose homeostasis.
source: Together, these results support a causal link between Adrb2-mediated control of the intra-islet vasculature via regulating VEGF-A expression during development and the later effects on adult β-cell function and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Inference based on rescue experiments with VEGFR2 blockade.

claim: Negative regulatory pathways are as important as positive pathways to counter un-restricted growth of tissues/organs during development.
source: During development, negative regulatory pathways are as important as positive pathways to counter un-restricted growth of tissues/organs.
evidence: General biological principle stated in the manuscript.

claim: Adrb2 acts as an endogenous 'brake' to curtail excessive vascularization during islet development.
source: Here, we reveal a previously uncharacterized role for β2-adrenergic receptors (Adrb2) in acting as an endogenous 'brake' to curtail excessive vascularization during islet development to thereby influence blood glucose homeostasis later in life.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the study findings.

claim: Adrb2, acting in β-cells, suppresses VEGF-A production to limit excessive intra-islet vasculature during islet maturation.
source: Our findings support a scenario (Figure 5) where Adrb2, acting in β-cells, suppresses VEGF-A production to limit excessive intra-islet vasculature during islet maturation.
evidence: Summary interpretation of the study findings illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Islet endothelial cells are critical for regulation of insulin biosynthesis in neighboring β-cells.
source: Islet endothelial cells are critical for regulation of insulin biosynthesis and exocytosis in neighboring β-cells.
evidence: Inference based on study findings and established knowledge.

claim: Islet endothelial cells are critical for regulation of insulin exocytosis in neighboring β-cells.
source: Islet endothelial cells are critical for regulation of insulin biosynthesis and exocytosis in neighboring β-cells.
evidence: Inference based on study findings and established knowledge.

claim: Loss of pancreatic Adrb2 disrupts the balance in bi-directional signaling between islet β-cells and endothelial cells.
source: Loss of pancreatic Adrb2 disrupts the balance in bi-directional signaling between islet β-cells and endothelial cells, resulting in hyper-vascularized islets and enhanced insulin production.

evidence: Inference based on MIN6 cell data and comparison with sympathectomy studies.
